pr_title: drivers: kscan: ft5336 hogs resources in interrupt mode
pr_body:
Allow the interrupt line to be used to correctly detect quick
press/release events, while using the timer to sample at a
configurable rate between the press/down and release/up events,
reducing resource use.

Fixes #33994

Signed-off-by: David Hoover <39233766+dhoove@users.noreply.github.com>

issue_context.title: kscan_ft5336 doesn't provide proper up/down information when polling, and hogs resources in interrupt mode
issue_context.body:
The 'pressed' value that is provided by the callback is only 1 if the touchpad was being pressed at the moment it was being sampled. If you press quickly between sampling periods, 'pressed' will always remain zero. One way to solve this problem is by activating interrupt mode. But in this case, the interrupts are generated at high frequency (approximatly 40Hz), causing significant I2C traffic and hogging resources.

To reproduce:
- set `KSCAN_FT5336_PERIOD` to 1000
- set `KSCAN_LOG_LEVEL_INF` to `Debug` so that you can observe the touch events in the log
- create a devicetree alias to `touch_controller` named `kscan0`
- make sure the touch_controller has a int-gpios line defining the IRQ line.
- make sure that touch_controller's i2c interface is up and running
- create the device with `device_get_binding(DT_LABEL(DT_ALIAS(kscan0)))`
- attach a callback with `kscan_config()`, and enable the callback with `kscan_enable_callback()`.
- observe the 'pressed' column of the log, while quickly touching and releasing the display. Most of the time, the `pressed` value will never change to 1.

This problem is disturbing because accurate press detection results in high CPU use, both in polling and interrupt mode.

I also have no understanding that one makes such an effort with macros just to save a few octets in RAM and flash. @jfischer-no, sorry if I clicked on 'resolve issue' when I shouldn't have. I was waiting for some feedback, and I though that maybe you were waiting for me to click on that in order to signal to you that I have addressed your concern.

I don't believe it's really possible to make this code simpler except by reducing the number of handled cases (which you mention). Currently, there are three cases:
- polling mode
- interrupt mode
- interrupt polling mode

Interrupt mode samples only at the highest possible sampling rate. For that reason, it is undesirable for low duty-cycle applications.

Polling mode has poor performance. But it should probably not be eliminated, because some hardware devices may not have a dedicated interrupt line.

Interrupt polling mode has configurable sampling rate, making it much more appropriate for low duty-cycle applications. I personally believe that interrupt mode is rendered obsolete by interrupt polling mode. But I didn't feel like it was up to me to make this decision and remove it. For this reason, I added the third case (interrupt polling mode), keeping the two others. This mode is by far the best solution for the case where only down and up events are necessary. It reacts immediately, and if the sampling period is set to 0, it almost always uses zero MCU time.

I don't understand why you say I made a massive effort with macros to save a few octets in RAM. I didn't do that at all. I simply added the third case in what I thought was a reasonably readable way, because I didn't feel like it was up to me to delete 'interrupt mode'. Of course, if you wish, I could remove the `KSCAN_FT5336_GPIO_INT_EDGE` and `KSCAN_FT5336_ENABLE_TIMER` defines which are the root cause of your apparent discontent. That would simply move the mess further down into the heart of the code, making easy-to-read code like the following much messier:
```
#ifdef KSCAN_FT5336_ENABLE_TIMER
	/** Timer (polling mode or interrupt polling mode). */
	struct k_timer timer;
#endif
```

Concerning your question about why KSCAN_FT5336_PERIOD exists in interrupt polling mode: it is used to select the sampling period. In 'interrupt mode', this is not configurable, and for hardware-related reasons, the device is always sampled at approximately 20ms.

In interrupt-polling mode, KSCAN_FT5336_PERIOD allows the developer to select an appropriate value to satisfy application requirements. If the developer selects zero, no sampling is done at all between down and up events, so the MCU use is almost always zero. Perhaps you could try out the code and compare the three modes while watching the SPI bus on a logic analyzer. The advantage of interrupt polling mode might become more clear to you.

What do you suggest I do? I personally believe that this code is an improvement over what was previously available. Would you like me to delete 'interrupt mode'? That would result in minor simplifications of the code, and I could then delete the additional #defines mentioned above that seem to disturb you. I don't really see the point. Despite the three cases, the file is reasonably readable. And there may be cases where the developer doesn't care about the MCU hogging that happens with interrupt mode, and wishes to sample at the highest possible sampling rate (I believe this could almost be achieved, however, by using interrupt polling mode with KSCAN_FT5336_PERIOD=1.

@MaureenHelm, @gmarull, do you believe that this driver handles too many cases, resulting in messy code? Should any of the three cases (polling, interrupt, interrupt polling) be removed?
